newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD-Tokyo stocks to search for direction.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Tokyo stocks to search for direction.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's benchmark is likely to consolidate this week after the Nikkei average fell below the psychologically important 18,000 level for the first time in nearly a month, brokers said.
The Nikkei 225-share average ended 157.41 points, or 0.87 percent, higher at 18,198.74 on Friday, but down more than 350 points on the week.
Brokers said the Nikkei average would likely waver between 17,300 and 18,500 in the coming week as financial institutions sell stocks ahead of the end-March corporate book closing.
"The Nikkei average is still in the 17,000 to 19,000 range it has been in for the past few months," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, Yamaichi Securities general manager.
After challenging the 19,000 level in late February, the index has slipped back about 1,000 points. But Kamogawa said it was trying to muster up the courage to make another challenge of the level.

Brokers said that although there had been intra-day falls below 18,000, the index had always managed to struggle back above 18,000 by the close, indicating support was fairly strong and the downside limited.
Investors will pounce on the shares of firms announcing revisions in earnings and on blue chips should the indices weaken greatly, they added.
With the passage of the fiscal 1997/1998 budget, traders also expect debate to increase over the use of public funds to pay off bad loans, and ways in which the liquidity of land can be improved.
"Deregulation measures and other changes in policies could be discussed by politicians and buoy the stock market as a result," said Akishige Ishikura, a Dai-ichi Securities analyst.

Traders will also be following news on Nomura, Japan's largest brokerage house. The 225-share Nikkei slumped to a low of 17,836.99 on Friday after news that Morua executives did irregular deals with a client apparently linked to racketeers.

The news once again threw a spotlight on the dark side of Japan's economy and also pointed to the tough road ahead as Japan tries to boost its financial industry's global competitiveness through a five-year "Big Bang" reform plan.

But several brokers said there were few real factors on the horizon to push cash stocks in any direction, but warned that movements in future contracts and arbitrage activity had the potential to send stocks reeling.

Uncertainties over the state of the economy in the new fiscal year, including the stifling effect of the two percentage point consumption tax hike, have been depressing futures prices in recent sessions.
The sudden falls had slowed the roll-over process of the March futures contracts ahead of the settlement on March 14, making it difficult to discern where the settlement price will be, brokers said.
"More position adjustment may emerge and there is a possibility that volatility of the index may increase," an official at Nomura Securities said.
